386.title: Peace between the two is better
386.hook: if a couple fear a rift, reconciliation is best (4:128)
386.howItsDone: Muslims practice sulh, reconciliation, in marriages, families and communities, often through elders or mediators, and Islamic law recognizes settlement as a way to end disputes, provided it is freely agreed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'adl: justice, even against yourself, your parents, your kin. Your line was justice, even against me.

Wa-s-sulhu khayr. In Arabic it's two words, with the and fused onto the first: and reconciliation is better. The phrase sits in a verse about a marriage going cold, but the word reached much further. Islamic law uses sulh for any settlement that ends a dispute, between neighbors, business partners, or whole families. A word about one marriage is also the word for peace between anyone. But first, the verse itself, which is surprisingly honest about why making peace is hard.
screen: `TWO WORDS.` → `A MARRIAGE GOING COLD.` → `WHY PEACE IS HARD.`

segments.voice: Verse 128 says: if a woman fears ill-treatment or turning away from her husband, there's no sin on them if they settle things between themselves, and reconciliation is better. Then a surprising line: souls are prone to stinginess. Shuhh: tight-fistedness, holding on to what you're owed. Each side clutches its rights. Then: if you do good and are mindful of God, God is aware of what you do. Sulh means settlement, peace-making, a deal that ends a quarrel: the opposite of insisting on every last right. A'ishah explained the verse, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari: it's about a husband who no longer wants his wife, and she says, keep me, and I'll give up some of what's due to me. Each gives something so the bond survives. Commentators connect it to Sawdah, one of the Prophet's wives, who gave her night to A'ishah so the marriage would continue. Scholars stress that a settlement must be freely chosen, never forced on the weaker side. And the principle spread far beyond marriage. In 49:10: believers are siblings, so make peace between them. A hadith in Abu Dawud reports the Prophet ﷺ asking: shall I tell you of something better in rank than voluntary fasting, prayer and charity? Setting things right between people. A hadith in Bukhari even says the one who reconciles people by passing on good words is not a liar. Reconciliation is better, the verse says. Not easier. Better.
screen: `A MARRIAGE GOING COLD` · `SHUHH: CLUTCHING YOUR RIGHTS` · `SULH: EACH GIVES SOMETHING` · `BETTER THAN EXTRA FASTING` · then, large: `AND RECONCILIATION IS BETTER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone close with whom there's distance right now, and name honestly what you're holding on to: the apology you're owed, the point you want conceded. Then ask what one thing you could let go of, freely, so the bond survives. If you pray, you can ask God to soften both hearts.
Sulh. Settlement, reconciliation: each side gives something so the bond survives, from 4:128, and reconciliation is better. Today's word.
Your line: reconciliation is better. Each side gives a little, and the bond survives. Day three hundred eighty-six, done.

387.title: Isa in the Qur'an's telling
387.hook: the Qur'an says Isa was not killed but raised to Allah, and calls him a word and a spirit from Him (4:157–158; 4:171)
387.howItsDone: Muslims honor Isa as a prophet and the Messiah, born of the virgin Maryam; the common Muslim reading of 4:157–158 is that he was not crucified but raised alive to God, hadith speak of his return before the end of time, and Muslims say 'peace be upon him' after his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sulh: settlement, each side giving a little. Your line was reconciliation is better. Today is the last day of an-Nisa.

Jesus, in Arabic, is Isa. Some people meet him in the Qur'an for the first time and are surprised at what they find. The Qur'an calls him the Messiah, al-Masih. His mother Maryam has a surah named for her. Muslims say peace be upon him after his name, as they do for the other prophets. Near the end of an-Nisa, two short passages give the Qur'an's own account of who he was, and of how his life on earth ended.
screen: `ISA, THE SON OF MARYAM.` → `AL-MASIH, THE MESSIAH.` → `TWO SHORT PASSAGES.`

segments.voice: The first passage, 4:157, answers a claim made by some in his day, that they had killed the Messiah. In Pickthall's words: "They slew him not nor crucified him, but it appeared so unto them." And 4:158: God raised him up to Himself. The common Muslim reading is that Isa was not crucified, and that God took him up alive. How it appeared so has been explained in different ways. One classical explanation is that someone else was made to look like him. Other commentators said only that the matter was made to seem so, without naming how. Some Muslim thinkers have read the verse differently again. And hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari speak of Isa returning before the end of time. Christians believe Jesus was crucified, died, and rose again, and that event is at the center of their faith. Here the two traditions differ plainly, and each holds its account with deep conviction. The second passage, 4:171, says who Isa is. In Pickthall's words: "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, was only a messenger of Allah, and His word which He conveyed unto Mary, and a spirit from Him." A word, kalimah. Muslims commonly explain it by 3:59: like Adam, he was created by God's word, be, and he was. A spirit from Him, ruh minhu. The same verse asks the People of the Scripture not to say three, and Christians, who understand the Trinity as one God, have long discussed this verse with Muslims. Both traditions call him the Messiah. Both call him a word. They mean different things by it, and it's worth knowing exactly what each one means.

Kalimah, a word. Isa, the Messiah, called a word from God conveyed to Maryam, and a spirit from Him, raised up to God. Today's word.
Your line: a word from him. And with that, the long walk through an-Nisa ends. Until tomorrow.

388.title: Fulfill your contracts
388.hook: O you who believe, fulfill your obligations (5:1)
388.howItsDone: Muslims treat contracts as religious obligations: marriage is concluded by an 'aqd, Islamic commercial law rests on honoring agreements, and 5:1 is often quoted on keeping promises and treaties.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kalimah: Isa, a word conveyed to Maryam, and a spirit from Him. Your line was a word from him. Today, a new surah.

The fifth surah is al-Ma'idah, the Table Spread, named for a story near its end, where the disciples of Isa ask for a table of food to come down from heaven. Tradition places it among the last surahs revealed. And it opens with a command of two Arabic words, three in Pickthall's English, right after the address. No story, no setting. Just a sentence that covers a marriage, a mortgage, a handshake and a treaty.
screen: `AL-MA'IDAH, THE TABLE SPREAD.` → `AMONG THE LAST REVEALED.` → `ONE SHORT COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Here it is, 5:1, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." The Arabic for undertakings is al-'uqud, contracts, plural of 'aqd. Arabic dictionaries trace it to a root for tying a knot. A contract is a knot tied between two parties, and the verse says: don't let it slip. Commentators read 'uqud widely: the covenant between a person and God, and every agreement between people, marriage, sale, rent, employment, oaths, treaties. Marriage itself is called 'aqd al-nikah, the knot of marriage. In 17:34, the Qur'an adds that the covenant will be asked about. The Prophet ﷺ faced a hard test of it at Hudaybiyyah. He had just agreed a treaty with the Quraysh of Mecca, and one term was painful: anyone who came over from Mecca to the Muslims without permission would be sent back. The ink was barely dry when a young Muslim named Abu Jandal stumbled into the camp in chains, escaped from Mecca, begging not to be returned. His own father, Suhayl, was the Meccan who had negotiated the treaty. The companions were in anguish. The Prophet kept the terms, and told Abu Jandal to be patient, that God would make a way out for him. The sira reports that the way did open: before long, the Quraysh themselves asked for that clause to be dropped. A contract kept only when it's convenient isn't really a knot. The verse asks for one that holds even when it pinches.
screen: `'AQD: A KNOT TIED BETWEEN TWO` · `WITH GOD, AND WITH PEOPLE` · `ABU JANDAL IN CHAINS` · `A KNOT THAT HOLDS WHEN IT PINCHES` · then, large: `FULFIL YOUR UNDERTAKINGS.`

segments.voice: List in your mind the knots you've tied: a lease, a job, a promise to a friend, a deadline, a commitment to someone you love, even I'll call you back. Notice, without punishing yourself, which are holding and which have quietly slipped, and which one has become inconvenient.
'Aqd, a knot, a contract tied between two parties. Awfu bil-'uqud: keep the knots you've tied, with God and with people, the opening of al-Ma'idah, 5:1. Today's word.
Your line: keep the contract. Small knots count too, like I'll call you back. That's day three hundred eighty-eight.

389.title: Help in goodness
389.hook: help one another in righteousness and mindfulness, not in sin (5:2)
389.tomorrow: Food of the People of the Book
389.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 5:2 for mutual aid, volunteering and charitable cooperation, and for refusing help in wrongdoing, even to friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'aqd: the knots you've tied, kept. Your line was keep the contract.

A friend calls late at night. I need a favor. Can you tell my boss I was with you yesterday? Can you lend me money, for the thing you suspect it's for again? Can you help me get back at my ex? Loyalty pulls one way. Something else pulls the other. The second verse of al-Ma'idah gives a short rule for it, and a hadith turns that rule into something surprising.
screen: `A FRIEND CALLS LATE AT NIGHT.` → `I NEED A FAVOR.` → `LOYALTY PULLS ONE WAY.`

segments.voice: Verse 2 begins with the pilgrimage: its sacred months, its offerings, the pilgrims on their way. It warns the believers not to let resentment toward the people who once blocked them from the Sacred Mosque push them into aggression. Then, in Pickthall's words: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty. Help not one another unto sin and transgression." Two Arabic words carry it. Birr, righteousness, a wide, warm word for goodness, the same word used for kindness to parents. And taqwa, mindfulness of God, the awareness that keeps you careful. So the verse doesn't say help your friends. It says help with good. The direction matters more than the person. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it vivid. The Prophet ﷺ said: help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or oppressed. The companions were puzzled. Helping the oppressed, they understood. But how do we help him if he's the oppressor? The Prophet answered: by stopping him. That's help, too. Sometimes the loyal answer to the late-night call is no, and then a better offer: I won't lie to your boss, but I'll help you talk to him. I won't lend you that money, but I'll drive you to the meeting. Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, says whoever points someone to good gets a reward like the one who does it. So helping in goodness isn't only refusing. It's also cheering, driving, lending, showing the way.

segments.voice: Think of someone trying to do something good right now: study, get healthy, quit something, care for a parent. Picture what they're up against, and one concrete help you could give, not advice but help: a ride, an hour, a meal, a message at the right moment.
Birr, a wide, warm word for goodness. Help one another in it and in taqwa, mindfulness of God, never in sin and aggression, from 5:2. Today's word.

390.title: Food of the People of the Book
390.hook: the food of those given the Book is lawful for you (5:5)
390.howItsDone: Muslims follow different scholarly views on eating meat prepared by Jews and Christians: some accept it, some ask how it was slaughtered, some prefer halal or kosher; pork and alcohol stay off the plate whoever serves them, and meals are often shared across faiths at holidays and iftars.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birr: help one another in goodness, never in sin. Your line was help in good only.

Food is where neighbors become friends. The plate of cookies at Christmas, the dish brought over after a funeral, the invitation to break the fast in Ramadan, the Passover meal a coworker invites you to. But for people who keep food laws, every invitation comes with a quiet question: can I eat this? Al-Ma'idah, the surah named for a table, answers part of that question, with a door held open both ways.
screen: `FOOD IS WHERE NEIGHBORS BECOME FRIENDS.` → `CAN I EAT THIS?` → `A DOOR OPEN BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Verse 5, in Pickthall's words: "This day are (all) good things made lawful for you. The food of those who have received the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them." Those who received the Scripture are the People of the Book, the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, met before in the common word. Notice the symmetry: a two-way table. The same verse permits Muslim men to marry chaste women from among the People of the Book, a permission that, for some readers, shows how close these households could be. What does their food mean exactly? Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abbas, reads it especially as meat slaughtered by Jews and Christians, since bread and fruit were lawful anyway. Here Muslim scholars differ. Some accept such meat broadly. Others require that it be slaughtered in the way of their own tradition, or that God's name not be replaced by another. Scholars hold that what's forbidden in itself, like pork and wine, doesn't become lawful because someone else serves it. In practice, Muslims handle this differently: some eat at any Christian or Jewish friend's table, some ask about the meat and choose fish or vegetables, and some buy kosher meat where halal isn't available. What doesn't differ is the hospitality. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says whoever believes in God and the Last Day should honor their guest. A verse about food rules turns out to be a verse about who you can sit down with.
screen: `ALL GOOD THINGS MADE LAWFUL` · `A TWO-WAY TABLE` · `WHAT THEIR FOOD MEANS: SCHOLARS DIFFER` · `HONOR YOUR GUEST` · then, large: `YOUR FOOD IS LAWFUL FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Picture a table with people from different traditions you know around it: a Christian coworker, a Jewish neighbor, a Hindu friend, someone with no religion at all. What would you cook so that everyone could eat, and whose table would you be glad to sit at?
Halal. What's lawful to eat; 5:5 says the food of the People of the Book is lawful for Muslims too, a table open both ways.
Your line: a shared table. Their food is lawful for you, and yours for them. Day three hundred ninety, done.

391.title: The wudu verse
391.hook: wash your face, your hands to the elbows, wipe your head, wash your feet (5:6)
391.howItsDone: Before prayer, Muslims perform wudu: washing the hands, mouth, nose, face and arms, wiping the head and ears, and washing the feet (Sunni) or wiping them (most Shia); when water can't be used, they perform tayammum with clean earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, halal: the food of the People of the Book, lawful both ways. Your line was a shared table.

Before prayer, in bathrooms, courtyards and airport washrooms all over the world, Muslims stand at a tap and go through the same quiet sequence. Hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, ears, feet. A stranger watching might think it's just hygiene, and it is clean. But it's also a passage from the ordinary into prayer. You met the word wudu back in year one. Today, the verse that sets it down.
screen: `AT A TAP, BEFORE PRAYER.` → `HANDS, FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` → `THE VERSE THAT SETS IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Al-Ma'idah 6, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, and lightly rub your heads and (wash) your feet up to the ankles." That's the core, four actions, in the order the verse names them: wash the face, wash the arms to the elbows, wipe the head, and the feet. The rinsing of mouth and nose, the ears, the repeating of each part, come from the Prophet's own practice, described in the hadith. Here's a detail worth knowing. The Arabic word for your feet can be read with two different vowel endings, and both readings are old and recognized. Read one way, the feet belong with the things you wash. Read the other, they belong with the head, which you wipe. Sunni Muslims wash the feet; most Shia Muslims wipe them. Same verse, two faithful readings. Then the verse makes room for difficulty. If you're ill, or traveling, or can't find water, use clean earth: tayammum, a light touch of the hands on clean soil, then over face and hands. And it ends: God doesn't want to make things hard for you; He wants to purify you and complete His favor on you, so that you might be grateful. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the inner side: when a believer washes the face, every wrong the eyes looked at leaves with the water, until he comes out clean. So the washing is written, step by step. And what it washes is more than skin.
screen: `FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET` · `WASHED OR WIPED: TWO READINGS` · `NO WATER: CLEAN EARTH` · `WHAT LEAVES WITH THE WATER` · then, large: `WHEN YE RISE UP FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If you make wudu, say the verse's steps to yourself at the next one: face, arms, head, feet. If you don't, picture water running over your hands, then your face, and let one thing you'd like to leave behind from today, a sharp word, a glance, a worry, run off with it.

Wudu, the washing before prayer, from a root meaning brightness and cleanness. Al-Ma'idah 6: wash the face, the arms to the elbows, wipe the head, and the feet; and if there's no water, clean earth. Today's word.
Your line: the washing, written. Face, arms, head, feet, and clean earth when there's no water. Until tomorrow.

392.title: Even with those you dislike
392.hook: don't let hatred of a people make you unjust, be just (5:8)
392.howItsDone: Muslim jurists and teachers cite 5:8 as the ground of fair dealing with opponents, in courts, in trade and in war, and it is often recalled when anger at a whole group of people runs high.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wudu: the washing, written. A week ends today: peace between two, Isa, contracts kept, help in goodness, halal, the washing. Now the line that holds them all up.

Scroll through your contacts and one name may make your shoulders rise. A coworker. An ex. The cousin who ruins every holiday. Now someone asks you to describe your last argument with them, and asks for one thing only: be accurate. Not kind. Accurate. Fair to the person you can't stand is a different muscle. Fair to a whole group you resent is harder still. Surah five was given to a community that had real opponents, people who had fought them and turned them away from Mecca. Twice in this one surah, the Qur'an stops to say the same hard thing about them.
screen: `THE NAME THAT MAKES YOUR SHOULDERS RISE.` → `NOT KIND. ACCURATE.` → `SAID TWICE IN ONE SURAH.`

segments.voice: First, verse two, three days back: don't let hatred of the people who barred you from the Sacred Mosque push you into wrongdoing. The second is verse eight, today's. In Pickthall's words: “let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.” The Arabic word for that hatred is shana'an, a deep, settled dislike, the kind that has history. The verse opens by telling believers to be qawwamin, people who stand up and keep standing, as witnesses for Allah in fairness. Set it beside 4:135, from a week ago: stand for justice even against yourselves, your parents, your kin. Commentators pair the two verses. One guards against bending the truth for the people you love. The other guards against bending it against the people you hate. Love and hate pull the scales in opposite directions, and the Qur'an names both. A hadith report tells of a companion, Abdullah ibn Rawaha, sent to assess a harvest at Khaybar for people who had been at war with Medina. He told them, more or less: I come from the person I love most, and you are not dear to me, but neither will make me unfair to you. They are said to have answered that this is what holds up the heavens and the earth. And notice the reason the verse gives. Not that your enemy deserves it. That justice is nearer to taqwa, to living aware of God. The fairness is about who you are, not about who they are.
screen: `SHANA'AN — A HATRED WITH HISTORY.` · `QAWWAMIN — THOSE WHO KEEP STANDING.` · `LOVE AND HATE BOTH TIP THE SCALES.` · `NEARER TO TAQWA.` · then, large: `DEAL JUSTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring that person to mind and try to say one true thing in their favor: not a compliment you don't mean, just something accurate, like they work hard, or they were right about that one thing. If nothing comes, stay with the breath and let the question sit.
Shana'an. The old, settled hatred the Qur'an says must never bend you from being fair, even to the people you resent.
Your line: just, even then. Love and hate both tip the scales. And that's another week.
